trick: The environment has a living half and a non-living half, and the exam word for them is biotic and abiotic. Anything that was ever alive — leaf litter, a dead log — still counts as biotic; sunlight, soil minerals and water do not.

trick: The Brundtland definition is worth memorising word for word: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It came from Our Common Future, 1987 — and the whole idea is an argument between the present and the future, not between growth and no growth.

trick: Renewable means it comes back within a human lifetime; non-renewable means it took millions of years to form and will not be replaced. Forests are the trap: renewable in principle, but only if you cut them slower than they grow.

trick: Poverty and environmental damage feed each other in a circle: the poor depend most directly on forest, water and soil, and damaged forest, water and soil make people poorer still. That circle is the answer to almost any 'explain the relation between' question in this chapter.

video.query: population poverty and environment relationship class 11 environmental science

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about population, poverty and the environment.

items.statement: The poor often depend directly on common natural resources for fuel and fodder.
items.why: With no purchased alternatives, firewood, grazing land and open water are what remain — which is why degradation hits them first.

items.statement: Population growth affects the environment only through the number of people.
items.why: Consumption per person matters as much. A small rich population can use more resources than a large poor one.

items.statement: The demographic transition describes a fall in death rates followed later by a fall in birth rates.
items.why: The gap between the two falls is when population grows fastest.

items.statement: Environmental damage is caused only by industry, not by poverty.
items.why: Both cause it, by different routes — industry through emissions and waste, poverty through pressure on land, forest and water.

items.statement: Improving women's education tends to lower the birth rate.
items.why: It is one of the strongest and best-established relationships in population studies.

chapter: International Conferences: Stockholm, Rio and Agenda 21
trick: Three cities, three dates, in order: Stockholm 1972 was the first, Rio 1992 produced Agenda 21, Johannesburg 2002 reviewed it. World Environment Day, 5 June, is the anniversary of Stockholm — which is the easiest way to remember that Stockholm came first.

video.query: stockholm 1972 rio earth summit 1992 agenda 21 class 11 environmental science

data.prompt: Put the international environmental conferences in order.

items.label: Stockholm Conference
items.note: 1972 — the first UN Conference on the Human Environment; World Environment Day dates from it

items.label: Rio Earth Summit
items.note: 1992 — produced Agenda 21, the Rio Declaration and the climate and biodiversity conventions

items.label: Kyoto Protocol
items.note: 1997 — binding emission targets for developed countries

items.label: Johannesburg Summit
items.note: 2002 — the World Summit on Sustainable Development, Rio+10

items.label: Paris Agreement
items.note: 2015 — nationally determined contributions to limit warming

trick: Each treaty owns one problem, and the name usually hides the clue. Montreal is the ozone layer, Kyoto and Paris are greenhouse gases, Basel is hazardous waste crossing borders, Ramsar is wetlands, CITES is trade in endangered species. Montreal is also the one usually called the most successful environmental treaty ever made.

Holding the rise in global temperature well below 2 °C

trick: Do not confuse the two holes in the sky. Global warming is greenhouse gases in the lower atmosphere trapping heat; ozone depletion is CFCs destroying a layer in the stratosphere that blocks ultraviolet. Different gases, different layer, different harm — and questions deliberately mix them up.

trick: Environmental education is not one subject among others — its stated aim is awareness, knowledge, attitude, skill and participation, in that order. It ends in participation because knowing about a problem changes nothing on its own.

items.label: Knowledge

items.label: Attitude

items.label: Skills
